short: Phoneme-onset events within words (M06) are ahead as a protocol; full-inventory classification predates it (Brumberg 2011); the 36% headline is consonants only, on hand-labelled onsets.
position: The paper [@mugler2014direct] changes one component, the decoder (M06), and it is ahead as a protocol: it classifies each phoneme as an event at its own onset inside spoken words, which none of 51 earlier intracranial speech studies does (pattern match, Appendix) and none of the read deciding priors does [@brumberg2011classification; @pei2011decoding; @leuthardt2011using; @tankus2012structured], confirming the authors' second "first" claim (Sec. 4), with above-chance results in four subjects. The full-inventory part is not new: Brumberg et al. classified 38 attempted isolated phonemes at 16–21% against 2.6% chance, which the authors cite (Sec. 1), so their ECoG-scoped "first" is the accurate one. The headline overreaches: "up to 36% accuracy when classifying all phonemes" (Abstract) is subject NU2's consonant accuracy (36.1%, Sec. 3.1). The strongest confound is the labels: every analysed phoneme, test trials included, sits on an onset placed by hand from the microphone (Sec. 2.4), and Wilson et al. [later] measured that audio-derived onsets and microphonic contamination both inflate overt-speech phoneme accuracy, modestly [@wilson2020decoding]. On a matched protocol, later intracortical arrays only nearly matched it [@wilson2020decoding]; today's decoders need no per-phoneme onsets [@willett2023high].
